At 4:17 in the afternoon, the rain stopped without announcing itself.

The city noticed slowly. A woman under a red umbrella paused at the corner and looked up. A bus driver leaned out of his window. Somewhere, a dog shook water from its fur and startled a flock of pigeons into the gray air.

On the seventh floor of an old apartment building, a man opened his window. The room smelled of dust, wet concrete, and the coffee he had forgotten to drink. Across the street, every window held a different kind of life: a blue television glow, a hanging plant, a child pressing both hands to the glass, a kitchen where someone in a yellow shirt moved from counter to counter.

He wondered how many people were, at that exact moment, standing in front of their own windows and thinking the same thought:

There must be more to this day than what has happened so far.

Below, the pavement reflected the sky so perfectly that the world appeared to have two horizons. A bicycle passed through both of them.

The man smiled, though he could not have said why. He put on his coat and went outside without an umbrella. At the bakery on the corner, the woman behind the counter handed him a loaf of bread still warm from the oven. He carried it home with both hands, as carefully as if it were a small animal.

That evening, he tore the loaf open. Steam rose from its center. He thought of all the invisible work required to make something warm: the yeast waking in the dark, the patient pressure of hands, the heat gathered and held, the long transformation no one could witness.

Outside, the city began to light itself.

One window, then another.

Not stars, exactly.

But close enough.
